title: Great Saltpetre Cave
summary: Great Saltpetre Cave in Rockcastle County was mined for saltpeter during the War of 1812, when British blockades cut off imports for gunpowder.
bodyMarkdown:
[Great Saltpetre Cave](https://grokipedia.com/page/great_saltpetre_cave) in [Rockcastle County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rockcastle_County,_Kentucky) was once one of Kentucky's most important industrial sites. It was also known as Kincaid's Cave and the Great Cave on Crooked Creek. Its value lay in the dry cave earth, which held calcium nitrate, or niter, the raw material for saltpeter, a key part of gunpowder.

Robert Baker found the cave in the late 1700s. A stream ran through it, and the passages were wide enough for oxcarts to haul material out. Inside, miners worked by torchlight, digging the soil and leaching the niter from it.

## Science and gunpowder

In 1806, Dr. Samuel Brown, a Transylvania University professor of anatomy, chemistry and surgery, gave the first scientific description of Kentucky saltpeter production in Philadelphia. He drew mainly on work at this cave. Saltpeter from the cave usually went to Lexington to be made into gunpowder.

Other Kentucky caves, including [Mammoth Cave](/stories/mammoth-cave-saltpeter/) and the caves at [Carter Caves](/stories/saltpeter-cave-at-carter-caves/), became part of that supply.

## The War of 1812

During the [War of 1812](https://grokipedia.com/page/War_of_1812), British blockades cut off saltpeter shipped from overseas. Sixty to seventy men worked the cave, and many of them were enslaved. A county history gives a slightly different figure of up to 72 workers, and dates the cave's development to 1804. Their labor made the gunpowder that free Kentuckians carried to war, a reminder that the state's war effort rested partly on people who had no say in it.

The cave was mined again, on a smaller scale, during the Mexican–American War and the Civil War. Union soldiers who worked it in the Civil War lived inside, since the steady 58-degree air was easier to bear than winter cold or summer heat.

## Visitors and damage

Until the 1970s, the cave was a commercial attraction. It hosted tours, ballroom dances, a museum and weddings. Visitors often broke off formations as souvenirs and wrote their names on the walls. The most famous name carved there is Daniel Boone's.

## Kentucky today

The cave lies within the Daniel Boone National Forest and joined the National Register of Historic Places in 2013. The Rockcastle Karst Conservancy owns it as part of the 300-acre Great Saltpetre Preserve. Overnight camping is possible on request, so the passages that once fed powder mills are now visited for their history and karst.
